Empirical Research Plan: Capitalization of Public‐School Characteristics into Housing Prices in Charlotte–Mecklenburg, 1994–2001
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy
   • Core design: “Boundary-Discontinuity Difference-in-Differences”  
     – Cross-sectional component: compare houses that lie very close to opposite sides of an elementary (or middle/high) school attendance boundary (a spatial RDD).  
     – Time-series component: exploit the large, sudden redistrictings in 1997 (high schools) and 1998 (elementary/middle) that reassigned roughly 30 % and 16–18 % of parcels.  
     – Estimator: difference-in-differences/event-study within ultra-local boundary pairs.  
   • Why appropriate?  
     – Houses mere yards apart share virtually identical neighborhood amenities, lot sizes, and zoning; the only systematic difference is the school to which they are assigned.  
     – Redistrictings generate plausibly exogenous within-house (or within-block) changes in assigned school quality, letting us difference out time-invariant unobservables.  
     – Combining the two dimensions isolates the causal effect of school attributes, controlling simultaneously for (i) neighborhood quality and (ii) endogenous household sorting.

2. Treatment and Control
   • Unit of observation: a sale of an existing single-family parcel i at time t.  
   • Treatment indicator  T_it: 1 if parcel i is reassigned to a different school in redistricting year τ and is observed in a post-redistricting sale (t ≥ τ); 0 otherwise.  
     – We will interact T_it with the change in an observable school characteristic ΔQ_i (e.g. change in mean grade-5 math score in SD units).  
   • Control group: parcels within the same 50–200-meter boundary band that remain assigned to the same school before and after τ.  
   • Timing: τ = 1997 for high-school treatment; τ = 1998 for middle and elementary treatment. A balanced ±3-year window (1994-2001) is used.  
   • Spatial running variable (for the RD side): signed perpendicular distance (meters) from the pre-1997/1998 boundary. The ±200-m window is narrow enough that, conditional on micro-location FEs, non-school amenities are identical.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
   A1. Parallel price trends within boundary pairs.  
        – Houses on the two sides of an attendance line would have continued to appreciate similarly absent reassignment.  
        – Plausible: lines are administrative, not coincident with physical barriers, and the sample window is short (3 yrs pre / post).

   A2. Boundary changes exogenous to micro-neighborhood trends.  
        – District cited capacity growth and court orders, not housing prices, when redrawing.  
        – New high-school openings affected lines county-wide, not specifically luxury or declining areas.

   A3. No simultaneous place-based shocks differentially hitting treated versus control parcels inside the boundary band (exclusion restriction).  
        – Checked via parcel-level permits and census block-group changes.

   A4. Limited residential resorting in the very short run.  
        – We study prices of sold houses, so composition could change, but (i) repeat-sales specs soak up house FEs; (ii) event-study pre-trends tests for anticipatory listing.

4. Main Threats and Mitigation
   T1. Anticipation or sorting by forward-looking buyers.  
       – Mitigate: drop sales occurring during the 12 months between announcement and implementation; test for abnormal listing volumes.

   T2. Boundary-based neighborhood investments (new roads, parks) coincident with redistricting.  
       – Mitigate: control for any new capital projects using county GIS shapefiles and include block-group×year FEs.

   T3. Measurement error in school quality (test-score noise).  
       – Mitigate: use empirical Bayes shrinkage (“school value-added”) and instrument ΔQ_i with the leave-one-year-out mean to reduce attenuation bias.

5. R Code Outline

```r
#############################################
# 0. Packages
#############################################
library(data.table)
library(sf)          # spatial ops
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional FE
library(did)         # Callaway-Sant’Anna event study
library(rdrobust)    # spatial RD robustness

#############################################
# 1. Load Data
#############################################
parcels   <- fread("meck_parcels_1994_2001.csv")       # parcel x sale
schools   <- fread("school_characteristics_1993_2001.csv")
boundary  <- st_read("attendance_boundaries_1993_2001.shp")

#############################################
# 2. Merge and Construct Variables
#############################################
# Spatial join: parcel to boundary-year polygon
parcels_sf <- st_as_sf(parcels, coords = c("lon","lat"), crs = 4326)
parcels_sf <- st_transform(parcels_sf, crs = st_crs(boundary))
parcels_sf <- parcels_sf %>%
              left_join(boundary, by = c("year","geometry"), suffix = c("","_sch"))

# Compute distance to (pre-redistricting) boundary line
boundary_96 <- boundary[boundary$year==1996,]
boundary_line <- st_union(st_boundary(boundary_96))
parcels_sf$dist_bd <- st_distance(parcels_sf, boundary_line, by_element = TRUE)
parcels_sf$inside_band <- parcels_sf$dist_bd < 200   # 200-meter band

# Attach school quality
parcels_sf <- merge(parcels_sf, schools,
                    by.x = c("assigned_sch","year"),
                    by.y = c("schid","year"),
                    all.x = TRUE)

# Treatment indicator
parcels_sf[, reassigned := assigned_sch_pre96 != assigned_sch_post97]      # example for HS
parcels_sf[, post := (year >= 1997)]
parcels_sf[, treat := reassigned * post]

# Outcome: log price
parcels_sf[, lprice := log(price)]

# Keep analysis sample
sample <- parcels_sf[inside_band == TRUE & year %in% 1994:2000]

#############################################
# 3. Main DID Regression
#############################################
# Two-way FE with boundary-segment FE
did_main <- feols(lprice ~ treat*delta_math_score |
                  parcel_id + year,          # repeat-sales spec
                  data = sample, cluster = ~boundary_segment)

summary(did_main)

#############################################
# 4. Event-study for pre-trends
#############################################
sample[, rel_year := year - 1997]             # 1997 = implementation
es_mod <- att_gt(yname = "lprice",
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "parcel_id",
                 gname = "reassignment_year",  # first treated year = 1997/98
                 xformla = ~0,
                 data = sample)
ggplot(ets(es_mod)) + geom_line()

#############################################
# 5. Spatial RD robustness (cross-section 1996)
#############################################
rd_96 <- rdrobust(y = sample[year==1996]$lprice,
                  x = sample[year==1996]$dist_bd,
                  fuzzy = sample[year==1996]$delta_math_score)   # fuzzy if using quality jump
summary(rd_96)
```

6. Expected Results
   • Sign: A positive shock to assigned‐school test scores should raise nearby house prices; a rise in minority share or FRPL share should reduce prices.  
   • Magnitude: Prior literature suggests 2–4 % increase in house value per 0.2 SD rise in average test scores. With a 1 SD improvement, we expect roughly 10 % price appreciation within the boundary band.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID context)
   C1: No differential pre-trends (Parallel trends) – 1  
   C2: Exogeneity of treatment timing – 0.5 (court-ordered but capacity motivated)  
   C3: No spillovers within neighborhood band – 0.5 (possible if parents lobby for boundary moves)  
   C4: Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA) – 1  
   C5: Correct functional form and inference – 1  
   Total ≈ 4/5 ⇒ design appears reasonably credible.

This plan leverages both space and time to pin down the causal capitalization of school quality into housing prices while directly addressing neighborhood confounds and household sorting.
